utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a quick -- I don't know how to call it, a question or a clarification. Good morning, Your Honours. Yesterday, we received a schedule, a court schedule, from which it follows that we will be working every day through the 1st of April in the morning and also the afternoons in this courtroom. We saw, given the pace, that the Prosecution could be finished by the 18th or, at the latest, by the 25th of January this year, and based on the schedule of this courtroom, it seems to us that, as far as our case is concerned, the continuous set of hearings has been envisaged without any breaks at any time. Mr. President, Your Honours, we do need certain breaks in order to be able to finish our case, in order to be able to contact the witnesses we have identified so far and the new witnesses which we have identified since, based on all the evidence and all the witnesses that will be called in this case and in the Prosecution case. So we would like to ask for a break in order to complete the preparations for our case. Mr. President, Your Honours, can you tell us whether we have understood the schedule properly so that we can file a motion in order to ask for the time necessary for us to complete the preparation for our case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Seric, to bring this question to the attention to the Chamber. As we understand, that time schedule is just a tentative one. And we also believe that it's quite reasonable for you to have some time to prepare your case after the Prosecution's case, which is also the practice before this Tribunal. As for how long that time will be, I believe that will be the subject of the Pre-Defence conference which will be scheduled after the Prosecution's case. That's all I'm going to say at this moment. If you have any suggestions about how much time you need to prepare your case, you may file a motion and make some suggestions about it. Mr. Usher, would you please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. THE COURT: Before we start, I just want to remind you that you are still under the oath. Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours, and thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Allow me to introduce myself. I represent the accused here, Mr. Mr. Mladen Naletilic, and I will be asking you certain questions. I'm going to try to frame them in such a way to receive as short answers from you as possible so that we can move forward. And will you please take into account that we are both working through the interpreters, so please bear that in mind and make breaks between questions and answers. Now, I'm going to move into my first area of questioning. If I understood you correctly, that is, your evidence before this Trial Chamber and the statement that you had given to the OTP, as an observer of the European Union, you spent a total of 40 days in the area of Mostar, from 24 May through 14th June continuously -- sorry, 14 July. Then you -- sorry, 14 June, and until the end of June, you were on vacation, then you could not re-enter Mostar when you returned and you only covered the Siroki Brijeg area.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's not correct, sir. My leave was in July, not in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: You said June, but it was in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right, it started on the 14th of July, and then it last until the end of July.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And after that, on the 22nd of August, you left Herzegovina, that is, you ended your mission. And in this period of time, you moved about the Siroki Brijeg area because you had no access to Mostar. Is that correct, that is, you never entered Mostar, either the east or the west side?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: About which period are you talking now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm referring to the period after you were unable, based on your own evidence, after you were unable to enter the city of Mostar, that is, to visit it.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: You mean after returning of my leave, my short leave, are you talking about that period?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I think that's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So my question first was correct in saying that you spent approximately a month and a half in the area, plus/minus a day or two?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, I didn't count all the days, but approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the reports that you were filing were based on the knowledge that you had, that is, in the period of -- while you were stationed there. In other words, your reports covered the period of that month and a half, approximately.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Your task was to report to your centre in Zenica, and they were to forward those reports to the European Union, the international community. And those reports were compiled by yourself with the assistance of others, or not, and they were based on what you, yourself, learned. You yourself are not an intelligence officer, you were not there as an intelligence officer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: It's not a military organisation, and ECMM doesn't have intelligence officers, so that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You said that you had an interpreter who were I think a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is it true -- is it correct that you deliberately did not want to take an ethnic Croat interpreter because you did not trust a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's not correct because we had three or four in Siroki Brijeg, all Croats, so we were the only one who worked with Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The majority of time, that is, until you were not given permission to enter Mostar, you kept ethnic Muslim interpreters; it was only at Siroki Brijeg that you had an ethnic Croat interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: It's not clear. Is it a question? I don't understand what you want to know. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, you had an exclusively Muslim interpreter until you were denied ability to enter Mostar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Let me make it very clear: We, as team M2, only worked with one interpreter when we went from Siroki Brijeg into Mostar. That means, working in Mostar on both sides, we worked with that interpreter. We picked her up every day in Mostar and brought her back before we went back to Siroki Brijeg. In all other cases in Siroki Brijeg, at the CC, we were working with the other interpreters that were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, in the statement you gave on 8, 9, 10, and 13 of August, 2001 - and I'm going to show you the statement in English so that you can follow - page 1, page 1 of your statement, fifth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Sorry, there is no page 1. Second. Second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Paragraph 5. In my Croat version, it says, "We deliberately had hired a Muslim interpreter because we were afraid that the Bosnian Croat interpreters would brief the Bosnian Croat leaders about us."

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you were not afraid that the Muslim interpreters could pass on information to the Muslim leadership?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct. Because she was living at the west bank and not on the east side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And she continued to live on the west side with her family normally?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I don't know. During my stay there, she was living on the west side, yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to verify that this interpreter was not a member of some kind of service? How did you find her? Who recommended her to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: We found her ourselves and asked her if she was willing to serve us as team M2 downtown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You had no knowledge that she may have been with the intelligence services of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You said, and it is of general assumption here, that your role was to have been impartial and objective as -- your being a member of the EU monitoring team, your sympathies were never tipped more towards the Muslim side than to the other side. You were always perfectly objective?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Later on when we address your reports -- I don't have that impression. It seems to me that you trusted anything that the Muslims were telling you and that you were questioning everything that the Croat officials were telling you and you did not trust them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Object to the statements and characterisation of counsel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And, sir, I apologise to you. It is just purely an impression of mine. Any comment -- you continuously made comments about statements of Croat officials that they cannot be trusted, and when you handle statements by Muslim officials, it seems as if you never placed such doubt on their statements. I will take you back to that when we go through your reports, but this is not -- this was not meant as personal comment regarding you. Would you be so kind as to tell me whether you managed to learn how many Muslim refugees were there in Mostar when you arrived there on 24th of May, 1993? How many Muslim refugees were in the city and how many Croat refugees were there.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: At first, a very short comment on your first remark. Unfortunately, what you saw in my statement were not all my reports. That means it was the investigation by the Prosecutor. So when you see all my reports, you see that we were also impartially dealing with remarks from the other side. That's one point. Secondly, about the refugees and displaced persons, it was actually impossible by us to have an exact number at that moment, so the numbers you find in the reports were set by the officials from both sides. We only learned the numbers in discussions and in question and answering with the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, the reports you drafted, you had drafted, did you turn them over to the OTP? I did not see all of them. Do the OTP have them or does somebody else has these reports that you had compiled?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, I found, on diskette, most all my daily reports myself, and that was a very good possibility to bring back everything that happened at that time and to recall what happened and what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And these reports are your personal property or do they exist somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, most of them, and my personal notes, are personal property, of course, yeah. And I don't know if the EU, for instance, or someone else has the completed files.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, during your tour of duty, were you able to learn the ownership of the apartments where the refugees moved in? Did you learn that about 10.000 apartments were vacated by the Serbs who had left and that the refugees, predominantly Muslim refugees, had entered those vacated apartments?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: We don't have that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So when you say that -- that is you personally, or if you heard that somebody had entered some apartment, you did not know whether the person was a proper owner of such an apartment, that he had entered it provisionally, or did they have a lease, or they had something called tenants' rights at that time. In other words, the State would turn over and give certain apartments to use to certain individuals during the period when they worked for a certain enterprise or certain institution. So did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, the cases we saw and were dealing with definitely belonged to people who were living there for a long time and were citizens of Mostar and living on the west bank for many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You investigated that and you can claim this based on your investigation, or somebody told you about this and you are saying it because somebody had told you this?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You've just prompted me to ask you something else. I'm going to show you later on something from your documents I'm going to go through, but Exhibit 456.4, there was a list, and the Prosecutor discussed this with you. There was a list of persons who allegedly had left Mostar, and you were given this list by Arif Pasalic, a long list. You had it in front of you yesterday. I think the Prosecutor showed it to you. Did you interview any of those individuals who allegedly were expelled?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, sir, when you are talking about the list - and I recall well there were 88 persons - we didn't. We did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That's right, 88. And you did not interview any of them. Did you manage to learn from others who also told you they had been expelled when they had arrived in Mostar because many were arriving from the Podvelezje area, that is, the Mount Velez area. As you know, the Mostar region is a sizeable region, and all Muslims fled the Serb aggression from the east side to the west side. You know, this is actually one city even though it has these two sections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology, Your Honour. I don't think it's Defence counsel's role to make factual assertions in the courtroom and give comments to the witness and ask the witness to comment on his assertions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's probably true, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I add, Mr. Krsnik, that this is the first time that this suggestion has been made, although we have had a large number of Muslim residents of Mostar who have given evidence of having been transported from one side to the other. You haven't made this suggestion to any of them, and we did warn you about this, that in cross-examination, you have to lay the ground. It's not enough to just do it in the Defence case. I just wonder why you didn't raise this question with any of the many witnesses who gave evidence before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Clark, with your permission, I had discussions with witnesses about this and I was asking them questions about the ownership of apartments, where they had come from, and then a number of refugees from the area of Podvelezje and Nevesinje, I did ask a number of witnesses such questions. Sorry. I only wanted to ask this witness, as an objective monitor of the EU, what he was able to learn within the month and a half that he spent in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I have no recollection of you asking specific witnesses that the Prosecution called, suggesting to them that they didn't have legal title to the flat. And I don't believe that a single witness who has been called by the Prosecution was unable to show that they had legal title to the flat from which they were evicted. I believe that there were witnesses at the very beginning of the trial who would have been in a position to assist you in relation to that. I think some early witnesses said that many refugees were housed in buildings and not allocated to particular flats from which they were evicted. So I believe that you're shifting the ground somewhat, but however, I understand where you're coming from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you have to ask your question in the form of a question rather than make a statement of yourself and ask the witness whether he agrees with your statement or not. Try to do it in the form of a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. Thank you for your suggestions and guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, let us move on to another subject. Witness, you said that when you came to Mostar, it looked like Beirut to you, where you had also served. That is, to say, it resembled Beirut in terms of the destruction you saw there. Do you know where to what extent Mostar was destroyed during the Serb aggression and to what extent it was destroyed during this conflict between the Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: When I came in, of course, the city was already, for a part, destroyed. I only can tell you about increasing of destruction during my stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, the intensity of the destruction, was it the same from the Croat and the Muslim sides, were exchanges of gunfire taking place every day?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Depends on the calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: First question: Exchange of gunfire, did it take place every day from both sides as far as sniper fire is concerned?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Shelling?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Depends what kind of shelling. Direct or indirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Of course, I'm not an expert, sir, Witness, for military matters. But first, directly.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, let me explain it to you. Directly was only done from the west to the east side because of the equipment. When we are talking about directly, we are talking about artillery, for instance, or hand-held weapons with direct line of sight. Indirectly, for instance, could be artillery but most of the time were used mortars. Mortars was used on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, in front of you, you have your statement, and you said there -- and now that you've given me this explanation, it's quite clear to me. It's much clearer. You said that they exchanged gunfire, mortar fire, 120 millimetres, and that the Croat side had weapons up to 120 millimetres. Does that mean that they had mortars or would that calibre imply guns, cannons?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: We are talking about mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mortars?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: In the area they had mortars up to 120 millimetres. That was the biggest calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Both sides, right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I know that 120 was on the west side. I don't know if they had 120 on the east side. I don't believe it. I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Witness, would you tell me whether you have any personal knowledge of whether the Serbs were firing at Mostar in the months of April and May? I'm sorry, this is April and May 1993, of course.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Let me read your question, sorry. Well, as you saw in the reports, I came to Mostar in late May, so when you are talking about April and May, before I came in, I don't know. I can't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I see that you were interested in quite a few things and that you had various sources. Did you hear that there had been shelling from the Serb side in the months of April and May, and that it was aimed at East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I know that we had some rumours, we heard some rumours about that. We never could actually confirm that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, when you visited East Mostar, did you compile information about the entirety of the situation? For example, did you visit detained, imprisoned Croats in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, and that is in one of my reports also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you talk to them freely, I mean the detained Croats, as you talked freely to people at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, tell me, in West Mostar, was there also a reduction of water as was the case in East Mostar, or was there an abundance of water?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Sorry. By my knowledge, sir, especially in the second half of June, also the water supply or the water in the west was not enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sir, could you please be so kind as to tell us whether you visited the 4th primary school in Mostar -- I beg your pardon, East Mostar, the 4th primary school, where Croat civilians were detained?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the 4th primary school. I don't know which building you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm talking about the building that is on the east side, in the old part. It was a primary school. It was a school that was transformed into a camp.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, when you are talking about the building in front of the HQ of the 4th Armija, then we are talking about the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This school was near the hospital in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: We only visit a place in front of the HQ what was used as prison, and we saw there prisoners and HVO soldiers at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, how many times was the HVO hospital on the west side of Mostar, how many times was it supplied with all necessary material that had been requested? You did have a list.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, on the west side, there was never a request to us to supply, and I believe that, on the west side, they had enough equipment and supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not following the interpretation. I'm sorry, now I'll start following the interpretation, too. I apologise. Obviously we have misunderstood each other. At the request of the hospital in East Mostar, due to a shortage of medicines and bandages and all other supplies, they gave you a kind of list. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: The east side gave us a list, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And then you went to the west side, and you talked to physicians, or rather, Dr. Bagaric and other doctors about the needs of the hospital on the east side. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct. We handed over the list to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And how many times were requests put forth and how many times did you get all the necessary equipment and how many times was it submitted to the hospital on the east side? I mean, things like this, were they given from the hospital on the west side to the hospital on the east side?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: By my knowledge, twice; two times, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, was a request also put forth for a joint hospital, and had this come as an initiative -- I know that you and I understand each other, so I'll try to shorten things. But we know the east/west decided to set up a joint hospital under the control of the Red Cross and other international organisations on the west bank.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct. That was one of the proposals, that it was the hospital in the confrontation line so that didn't work, of course, and nobody was very in favour to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Before that, was there an initiative that doctors from the west side should go and work in shifts on the east side but they had refused that because they feared for their safety and security on the east side? They were afraid that they would be arrested by the Muslims? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, that was one of the points they brought up, they brought up. Actually, they were willing to do it, but there were a lot of points they brought up. One of the points was the security on the east side and, secondly, the security on the west side when they should go there. So they needed, of course, security from the Muslim side, but also from HVO side. And I know, because we worked a long time on this issue, that the east side was willing to do that, of course, because their situation was very, very bad. And HVO, at the end, didn't agree upon safetiness for their property and family on the west side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was this the HVO or personally the doctors? Was it the doctors themselves who expressed their dissatisfaction because they didn't want to go to the other side because the Muslim side would not guarantee their security, so it's the doctors personally not the HVO? That is to say, doctors from the west side did not want to go to the east side, they personally refused to go because the Muslim side, through your joint commissions that you always try to organise, did not get guarantees for their personal safety.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I think I have to read your text first. Let me make it very clear: The doctors were willing to do that. We had a list of doctors. They want to do that on a voluntary base but they needed from the authorities on both sides, guarantees, and an escorted transport from the west to the east and way back by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, I have been thinking about a question. Since you have a lot of experience, since you spent time at many places where there were wars, civil wars, et cetera, this example that we have been discussing so far, is it typical for a situation of civil war, or, perhaps, was this a situation where, in order to implement the Vance-Owen Plan, these conflicts simply could not be stopped, then, in the month of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know -- I'm not sure what the question is. We've gone from his other involvement around the world in other situations and now we're back to something about the Vance-Owen Plan. I object to the form of the question. I don't know what the question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, your question is very complicated which will confuse not only the witness but also us. Simplify your question and pose it in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So Witness, to the best of your knowledge the situation in Mostar, was it a typical situation for a civil war?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's very hard to answer because you can't compare it with any other place, but what I saw, and you are right, I saw some other places, this was a very complicated but crazy situation for sure. If that helps you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, just so the record is clear, the Prosecution does not concede in any way that this was only a civil war, despite the fact that counsel might want to couch his questions that way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I truly do not understand this intervention made by my learned friend. It wasn't an objection. It is simply the Prosecutor making a thesis of the OTP quite clear to the witness. I have asked this witness of his opinion on the basis of the experience he had had. At any rate, I thank you, sir, for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I simply asked you so that we would know, for example, whether in Beirut the Christian and Muslim militias would allow each other to visit each other's hospitals, to give assistance in terms of medical supplies and things like that. This question did have a point, but at any rate, I find your question -- your answer satisfactory. Another question now. Did you notice that everybody was armed, that each street had its own commander, that each village had its own commander? To put it this way: That there were thousands and thousands of big and small warlords on both sides.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, why do you disagree? Did you manage, in your work, in the course of your work, to notice any such things? And now since you've expressed your disagreement, could you please be so kind as to tell me why you disagree?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Because on both sides, there was an organisation, a good organisation, and authorities claimed that they had the situation on their own side under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, sir, in your reports and in the statement you made here, it seems obvious that officers themselves were saying that they did not have some units under their control.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, first, your question was speaking about thousands and thousands. That's a lot. Secondly, I made very clear that answering our questions by saying, "It was maybe done by criminal elements we don't have under control," of course that is an answer, but it doesn't mean that it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much for having helped me once again. Of course, when I said, "thousands of warlords, big and small," I meant the area that you had passed through and where you were. Of course, perhaps in Mostar and in that area, there could not have been thousands, but there were some that no organisation managed to control. Did you manage to find that out during the time you spent in the area?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Let me read your question once more, please. Well, I'm only talking about the Mostar area, and we were dealing with the official authorities. And of course I know there is a difference between combatant and non-combatant. We were aware of people in the area who were non-combatant but had influenced or influenced the situation over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, sir, Colonel, I'm asking you this because I think that we did not have the opportunity of discussing this very much. I think that you are only the third person we have here who has had such remarkable training as a person being trained at the Royal Dutch Academy. How much time does it take to establish an army? If we were to start today, if today were to be day one, with your knowledge and with your experience, how much time would it take for you to say, right, this is an army now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, Your Honours, perhaps I have not phrased this question very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But for example, in 1992, if people say, "We have to fight," when can they say this is a serious army? Is it an army that resembles the Royal Dutch Army or the British army or some other army of some other country? I think we need to clarify that situation. That's why I'm putting this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, I think we're getting far afield. I think if defence counsel rightly want to put questions to this witness about the chain of command concerning his client, that might be appropriate, and if there is an assertion, based upon some foundation, that his client, Tuta, did not have control over certain elements or something such as that, then he can put those questions to this witness. But now we are talking in broad generalities which I think, I submit, don't take us very far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we also believe that your question is not that relevant to the very case. So would you please ask some direct questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. Let me just respond to my learned friend. As for my client's place in the chain of command, I'm expecting him to provide evidence to that effect, and it is only then that I shall try to counter this through witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So, Witness, can you give me a very brief answer: Was this an organised army that you as a person coming from a western army, with all the traditions that you have in the military, could you say, with all of that in mind, that this was an organised army?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, again -- excuse me. Again, Your Honour, I object. Is he saying was this a NATO army? Was this an army by NATO standards? By what standards are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that Mr. Krsnik is flouting this very issue, but his question is not that proper. You have to rephrase your question in a more specific way so that everybody knows what kind of army you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is very hard because the Prosecution claims that this was an organised army and those of us who lived there and who were actually members of this army, it is very hard to qualify it as such. It cannot be compared to either the NATO system or the Warsaw Pact system, for that matter, or the U.S. system. The people simply organised themselves and went to war. So I don't know how to frame my question and so I'm proceeding in a very cautious way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So in your opinion, did this army even approach any military standards, either the NATO or Warsaw Pact, or can one say in that regard that the HVO was an army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, before the witness replies, the difficulty we're having is we don't know which army you're talking about. You keep talking about "this army." Which is the army you're talking about? If you clarify that, maybe the Witness can respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your intervention. I may have omitted but I was referring to the HVO. I may have even said -- I think that I had started out discussing that.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, sir, when I'm talking about army, I'm talking about combatants wearing uniforms. As you know, you can recognise them as a member of such an organisation, and it's my impression that the HVO was well organised as a military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was organised. And how did it function? That was my question. Did it function as, let's say, a Dutch army?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: You can't compare it, because the Dutch army was not in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Fine, let's move on. I was under the impression that I had asked an easy question. Here, my colleague gave me an excellent idea. We can compare the HVO and UNPROFOR. Were they in the same situation?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: In my perspective, you can't compare this because they had a complete other mission. So when you are talking about military organisation, then you have to go a little bit further. It's not so easy as you think that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know how many trained officers were there in the HVO, the ones who had completed officer training, either for commissioned or enlisted officers?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: We spoke to officers who had a regular training, and there were officers who did the former Yugoslavian academy, military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Of course there were several of them, but my question was a number. Of course, you are not in a position to know this. Will you be so kind as to tell me whether you knew the organisational structure of the HVO? What was the chain of command pyramid there?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, it's all in my statement, and our original structure by UNPROFOR which shows very well how it was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, my intention was to ask you what UNPROFOR produced was not what you produced. You may have been using it, and you may have informed yourself of it. Is that correct? You personally, when you contacted with people in Mostar over that month and a half, in that crazy situation, as you described it, what was the chain of command there? With whom could you talk? I mean, how did you understand who was in command there?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, I told you yesterday who I talked to, so you know it. And you know also who they were in the chain of command, I suppose. So when you think that I can recall the exact structure of HVO at this moment, then unfortunately I can't, but not at this moment after eight years. But you can use the information of UNPROFOR, what was updated every day, and very reliable also for us. By the way, we were actually -- what I told before -- a political instrument and, of course, dealing with military authorities, so we were more interested actually in the political issues. Because we had to deal with military authorities, we were very well informed about organisation and structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. On the basis of your reports and your statement to the OTP, my understanding was that you spoke to four or up to five persons at the most. They included Bruno Stojic, Mr. Coric - one was the Minister of Defence, the other one was in charge of the military police - Puljic and Maric, and then you had a meeting with Mr. Prlic, who was the president of the HVO, and Mr. Zubak, who was the vice-president; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Correct. There was a lot more, but that is what is mentioned in the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, could I make a suggestion to you. You may refer to the Exhibit P532.1, which was a charter indicating the commander chain, and the Prosecutor asked some questions to this witness about this charter. If you have any questions challenging this document, you are entirely entitled to ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, let me start in this way:

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, tell me, yesterday the Prosecutor showed you a picture. I'm going to show it to you again and I'm going to ask you some questions. This is Exhibit P36.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the kind assistance of the usher, may the witness be shown this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you gave evidence that you contacted Mr. Maric the most. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you had the most meetings with him, you met with him even daily, and you had one of the better cooperations with him, in your own words.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: We saw him many times because he was the spokesman of the HVO headquarters for some time, and he was a member of the joint committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In this photograph, you marked him with the number "1." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, if I were to tell you that this was not Stanko Maric, what would you say to that? Are you 100 percent certain?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: This is a man I saw many times, I spoke to, and by my knowledge, it is Maric, Stanko Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, this man is Mr. Vice Vukojevic. He is the president of the Constitutional Court of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, then, they look very alike, if that's the case. Maric was bald-headed and looking like this man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, could you clarify exactly who you say that person is because normally it's not important in the transcript, the spelling, but I think in this case we ought to know exactly who you say that person that is. If you don't mind, would you spell out his name and his title.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His name is V-I-C-E, first name, V-U-K-O-J-E -- V-I-C with the diacritic, for the interpreters, V-U-K-O-J-E-V-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In 1993, I don't know exactly what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not right still? V-U-K-O-J-E-V-I-C. I'm told by my colleagues that now it has been corrected. I don't know what his position was in 1993, but we will provide that information, what it was in 1993. But for the last three years, for sure he has been a Judge on the Constitutional Court of the Republic of Croatia. And he was definitely a representative or member of parliament of the Croatian parliament before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you see the person next to Mr. Vukojevic, the one right next to him? The one who is taller and who has a beard, next to the person to whom you referred as Mr. Maric? Witness, you need to look at the picture. I don't think that you can see it well on the monitor. So the first one.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you had never met him. And you marked Mr. Andabak with number "2." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, tell me, in your statement and in your reports, did you not in several places -- in your reports it is in three places, that he was a commander of the special units of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you learn -- first let me ask you, do you know who Mr. Juka was? What was his last name, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: We learned that, as I stated yesterday, Juka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, but his full name.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, but I don't recall his full name at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And do you know what his ethnic background was?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I think that he came before he went to Mostar from Sarajevo. But you mean his ethnic background, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you hear that Mr. Arif Pasalic had him arrested and that he issued an arrest warrant against him?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you know about a conflict that they had, that is, Mr. Pasalic and Juka, that during the arrest, and that a grenade was tossed in a container by Juka, and this container was in front of the army headquarters? Did you know about this personal conflict that they had?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: First, I don't know -- sorry. First, I don't know about which period you are talking. But we were not aware of this story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, I am referring to May 1993 but this may have been before your arrival there, that is, the conflict between Juka. So I thought that perhaps you had heard about this because everybody in Mostar knew about it, so I thought that perhaps your interpreter may have told you about it. Witness, let us move on. My next question is you said that you were shot at from the blue building, that is, that a rocket was fired and exploded 3 metres away from your car. Were you in the vehicle or were you in the building when this explosion took place?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: We were in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So from where did the fire come? And these are your assumptions and your inferences, so can you tell us where did this shell or rocket come from?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Not our assumptions, but that what we noticed, what we saw, and the only possibility was from the blue bank building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And it could not have come from any other position?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: No, sir. Impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How far was the blue bank building from the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Are you talking about the hit, sniper hit, or the rocket? Projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Projectile.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Very close, very close, because it was one of the -- I think also old school building where we had previous the joint committee meetings, and that was very close. Actually, more or less in the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: There were buildings at the confrontation line that were controlled by the Muslims along the Bulevar, and most of them actually along the Bulevar, along the line of confrontation, were controlled by the Muslims, and the blue bank building was a very small one. It was very close by. And let me show you a picture so that I make it easier for you.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, you don't have to show me the picture because when you are talking about the incident with the projectile, that was on the western side of the blue bank building. We knew the positions on the west bank of the Muslims quite well, which buildings they were occupying. It was impossible to have line of sight to the place where our car was located and where the impact was found by us, noticed by us. So your suggestion that it could be the other side is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, my suggestion, Witness, was not that the other side had fired it. You may have misunderstood me. I simply wanted to say -- actually to ask whether you were 100 percent certain of it or whether there is any space open for discussion of it. I just wanted an honest answer from you, so I respect your answer as you've given it. Now, as regards the sniping, are you 100 percent sure that it was also fired by the HVO, or that it came from the west side? In other words, did you ascertain where the shot had come from?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Actually, by the position of the car, by the angle of the bullet and the place it hit the car, it's by line of sight only possible from the blue bank building. So when you are talking about my military experience, that was the only possibility by my military knowledge of such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Of course, and I thank you. But when you heard that hit, and we can go back to your statement, but I think you recall it, you gave the statement in August, you stated that you had stopped the car, come out, looked at it.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, we passed first the Tito bridge, looked for a safe place, and then inspected where the impact was. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, in your experience, was a special war also waged in Mostar while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "special war".

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, everything that a special war entails; misinformation, counterintelligence, confusing the enemy, false information and so on, so we all know what "special war" means.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, that's a problem, I think, because I never heard of a special war, that -- you have to be specific, and maybe it's by a lack of knowledge about the right terminology. But can you explain me what you mean by "special war"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Of course, Witness. This is -- these were the terms that we used in our schools. When you say "special war", it's a war that is waged mostly by intelligence services which was to confuse the enemy, to plant misinformation, deception, all kinds of things that have been done during a war, unfortunately, throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, Your Honours, that we have already passed the break time, and it's time for break, so I'm going to get to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: If you were to analyse what you learned from Arif Pasalic, could it have been a part of a special war that all the information that was presented to you was to present the Muslim side in as favourable light as possible and to denigrate or otherwise harm the other side?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: We never got that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have actually gone past 11.00, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, will you show the witness out of the room first. So, we will resume at 11.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Witness, I think that we broke off when we were discussing questions related to special warfare, so I would like to proceed from there. Tell me, during the month of June, you were in Mostar every day, and your interpreter was with you all the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that she was one of your major sources? At that time, I mean, during the month of June?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: She was a part of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it is the duty of an interpreter to interpret, not to be a part of a team in the same way in which you were part of a team and Mr. Jesus?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood me. I mean a part of the team as interpreter. So I agree the only thing she did was interpretation, translating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Also, she provided information to you, the information that she wanted to provide to you. Had she not provided you with that information, you would not have had it. Right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: She told us, when we asked her about the situation during our absence in Mostar, sometimes what was happening, and most of the time, she was warned or told by other people what happened during our absence. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I think my question was clear. Had she told you that she knew nothing, then you would not have been at a few locations, and you would not have known about some of the cases that you did write reports on and that we're going to refer to right now. Isn't that correct? Let me help you with this. She was the one who took you to the apartment that you discussed yesterday with the Prosecutor. She told you that the Ministry of Defence is Mr. Naletilic's office. She took you to the position where allegedly there was this family, Alikafic, if I'm not mistaken, this burned house that you never found. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, it's partly correct. The last case, for instance, she was only translating the note that was brought to us through an individual on the west bank, and then we drove to that location. Talking about the apartment, she told us about the apartment, and the next step of us was, of course, to visit the place because, in such a case, she was a source confirming information we got from others, and we only tried to confirm and get from different sources as much as possible information about the same events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: For example, this apartment that you went to see, did you find out whose apartment this was, when this event had occurred, which army was involved? Was it perhaps an event that had taken place several months before that? Were there Serbs perhaps in that apartment? What was the name of that family who had done that? Did you find all of this out personally, or did you rely on the information that was provided to you by your interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: No. We went to there because she was tipped, and for instance, the door was opened by the next neighbours and they told the story. So they saw what happened and they heard what happened. So it was from firsthand, actually, at the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who were these neighbours?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, as far as I have details, you find it in my report. I can't recall that at this moment, of course. You will understand that, after eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Certainly, Witness. But the name of that family is not in your reports either, and what surprises me is that they have the keys to the apartment; I mean the neighbours. If they were ethnic Muslims, how come they had not been expelled, too? I just want to say to you, Witness -- I mean, the Trial Chamber always cautions me that I should perhaps explain why I'm putting a particular question. Did you, perhaps, think along the following lines, that all of this was staged for your benefit so that you would send a report to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: No, we never had that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think counsel is correct, that Your Honours, and particularly Judge Clark, has sometimes tried to assist counsel in putting his questions. I may be mistaken myself but I think the proper way to put this question would be, "We put it to you that it's the Defence case that the ransacking of this apartment was staged." And if counsel has a bona fide basis to assert such a thing and put it to this witness, then it's proper to do so. But to ask pure speculation is not the proper way to put the question, I don't think, and I defer absolutely to Judge Clark on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I agree entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it is pure speculation, Mr. Krsnik, but the witness has answered this question. You may move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I just say something, Mr. Krsnik. There are a lot of facts asserted by you in the question that you put or the statement that you made. First of all, what is the source of the information which you just put to the Court that the neighbours who confirmed the story which was being investigated were, in fact, ethnic Muslims? How do you know that? So can I take it that you're putting questions to this witness purely on a speculative basis and with no information behind you and no instructions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I do beg your pardon. Perhaps my question was, indeed, a bit confused. In the report I did not find the names of the neighbours, and the gentleman did not put down the names of the neighbours, and the source is primarily the lady interpreter. I just wanted to ask the witness what his personal knowledge was, who had been in that apartment? Whether he found out about that personally. When had that happened, when had the shooting taken place, the firing into the ceiling. Is this personal knowledge that our witness has or are these speculations that he simply espoused and then put into his report. Nothing else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, it goes much further than that. This witness has given evidence of inferences which he drew from facts that he found, that a complaint was made, a note was received about the fact that some people had been burned to death. He went to the area, he found that soldiers wearing HVO uniforms were posting on trees obituary notes relating to these people who had died. Yes, that's what he said. So the inference can be drawn that these people did die. And you are now saying -- you're going much further and saying that -- you're asking him did it occur to him that these deaths never in fact occurred and this whole thing was stage-managed? That's what the transcript says and that's what I heard, that the whole -- and that's what Mr. Scott is referring to, that the deaths were stage-managed. What are you in fact saying, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this is a major misunderstanding. I'm talking about two different events. I have now restricted to myself to the apartment where bullets were found in the ceiling that were photographed by the witness. I exclusively referred to that event. Now I had intended to move on to this other event, this other event that you had just referred to, and now I want to move on to that line of questioning where allegedly a family had been torched in their own apartment, and indeed, I thought after completing my questions related to the first event, and I asked whether this had happened a year ago, whether it was perhaps Serbs that were involved, et cetera, that is what I had meant, and these were questions related to the first event. I did not move on to the second event at all. So was this ethnic cleansing, that these people had been evicted? This is the first event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You didn't make it clear. You're talking about going to visit the scene. I thought you were talking about the more serious event and it's not clear. But one way or the other, the principle is the same, Mr. Krsnik. If you put questions to this witness, suggesting to him that he failed to investigate a setup, and you suggest to him that it was a setup, you must have information to back up that suggestion. It cannot be purely speculative. Do you understand the point that the Court is making? That you can't just throw out a question on the basis of something that could have happened when you don't have information to back it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. The background of this question was from my point of view, and I thought that that is the way I started it, that the interpreter, as I said at the very outset, and the witness told me the beginning also that they had not checked out her background, and the witness said no, and I asked whether she was perhaps a member of a particular service and the witness said that they did not check this, and they did not know, and then my last questions had to do with the special war. And the background to this question was that the interpreter, perhaps, might have been used in special warfare. Now, this is the background of my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you have information in relation to that or are you just fishing? Do you have specific information that this interpreter was engaged in the war by being a member of some secret services? You see, Mr. Krsnik, counsel must never personalize the cross-examination. Your view is irrelevant to this Court. We don't want to know what you think. You have to act on the instructions of your client and on the information which you have and the case you are going to make. This trial is not about what Mr. Krsnik thinks could have happened in Mostar. We're not conducting an inquiry in relation to your political or other views.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no political views. I just have information. Of course, when the time comes for presenting our case, we will try to show that the Muslim secret service always tried to reach international organisations, and I think that we have seen documents, too, that these secret services tried to get their people in, especially interpreters. This is not the Krsnik case; this is based on the information I have received and that I shall provide to this Court. I asked this witness quite fairly about whether there were any checks that had been made because it seems quite clear, Your Honour, that this interpreter was the main source of information for this witness. And this is how I understood it. As for my own political views, Your Honour, I have never, ever propounded them in this courtroom nor do I have any, for that matter. I think that I have already referred to this before this Court recess, that I was never a member of any political party and, notably, I said that I never intend to become a member of any political party. Because my basic personal belief is that a decent person cannot be involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I hope for your sake this isn't going to be transmitted in your country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since there's not a single journalist here from my country, and they are not following this trial at all, they usually transmit only what has to do with witnesses. It's the Muslim television that has been showing this particular footage time and again, this witness and what you said in relation to that. Unfortunately, nothing else is being transmitted from this courtroom. At any rate, I thank you for your suggestions and I shall certainly abide by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Then my next question would be -- I mean, now we are moving on to this other event when you got that note from that child, when you were going to check what had truly happened to this family that had allegedly been torched in their house, the house had been torched as well, and then you never found that house. Yesterday, you said that you saw HVO soldiers that were putting notices, death notices, on trees. Tell me, why did you not ask these soldiers or the neighbours or anybody where this house was and what had actually happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, we did, but we couldn't find.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. In your statement, you said something different. Just give me some time to find the exact page. In your statement, you said that you didn't want to ask Croats because it was primarily Croats who were living there and you didn't want to ask them for that reason because you were sure that you would not get an answer. Let me just find this in your statement now, the statement that you gave to the OTP in the month of August. Here it is, this is page 16 in the English version and page 15 in the Croatian language, the last paragraph. It's the last paragraph, and it says -- oh, page 16, the second paragraph on page 16. It starts in the following way: "We drove to the neighbourhood of Ilici that is mentioned in this note. That part of West Mostar was far from the front line and mainly inhabited by Croats." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, because we are talking here about the spot and the location where we were looking for. So this is correct. But I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, no, let's go on. I do beg your pardon for having interrupted you. We could not ask anybody where the burned house was, and we also did not expect the Croats to tell us where it was. In the quarter, we found the obituaries of this family on the trees. As a matter of fact, we saw the HVO putting these obituaries on the trees. Our interpreter went out of the car to read the obituaries and confirmed that it was about the death of the family Alikafic. So you did not want to ask the Croats and the interpreter confirmed this to you. You personally did not see this. You did not even find out which family this was. You mean you personally did not. Right?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I think we are talking about different things. When I am saying "confirmation," it means that we tried to figure out also in other places in West Mostar if they know something about this family. This is on the spot, and what is written here is what happened actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you assert that you did not expect the Croats to tell you where the house was. Obviously, you knew this from the very outset. "We could not ask anybody where the burned house, and we also did not expect the Croats to tell us where it was."

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: There were at the spot no people to ask. Then only the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I think that the two versions, the English and the Croat versions of your statement, are identical here. Did you say what is stated here?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I don't know if it's identical because I don't know your text. But my text here is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, I just read to you twice what it says. Is it identical?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, I still don't understand what your point is actually. I think it's clear what happened there. It describes exactly what we did, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, exactly. You did nothing. You did not establish what had happened, you did not find out what happened to them, you did not find out what their name was.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, we found out that the name was on the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Which was confirmed to you by your interpreters. You personally did not see this obituary, nor did you read it?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, I don't read the local language over there. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, why did you not ask the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, I think that we were not able to do that at that moment. I don't recall it, but you have to understand that not everyone was willing to speak with the man in white. Do you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah, yeah. [Interpretation] Of course, Witness. Will you please tell me now and confirm to me that you had a meeting with Mr. Slavko Puljic who was in the -- on the staff of the HVO armed forces. Did you ever talk to this man?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, did he also warn you about the special warfare and that he had information that your vehicles were stolen, were being stolen and used for sabotage operations and then the HVO was being accused of conducting them?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Can you be specific because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did Mr. Puljic tell you and did you write in your report, and there's a detailed report on what transpired in that meeting with Mr. Puljic, and your statement also contains it, that Mr. Puljic informed you that four vehicles -- four UNPROFOR vehicles had been stolen, with special markings and everything, and that these vehicles were used for sabotage and terrorist acts against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, if it's stated in my statement, in my report, then of course he told us that. You are talking about UNPROFOR cars. We were not UNPROFOR, of course, but ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I know, Witness. Here in your statement, it is -- in the Croatian version, it's page 17. In English, I assume it's going to be page 18 but let me give you the reference of the report. Sorry, it's on page 17. That is, you already had a report and you were surprised that Mr. Puljic did not know this, that is, you had the report that four UNPROFOR vehicles or your vehicles -- I don't know which one -- but you're referring to UNPROFOR vehicles, had been stolen by the Mujahedins, car-jacked, they were, in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: You are mixing the facts now as well as Mr. Puljic did at the time. By our information, we didn't know about four UNPROFOR cars, we only knew, of course, our own car who was hijacked in the Jablanica area from our team M1, the team in Jablanica, and that is exactly also what is stated here in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: For the Trial Chamber, can you clarify this; your vehicles were marked in a special way?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I explained that yesterday, yes, sir. We had nothing to do with UNPROFOR. We were marked with very big orange letters "ECMM," and UNPROFOR, of course, was in blue, marked "UNPROFOR." And we are talking about complete other vehicles. Our vehicle was only one hijacked and stolen in the north, and you are talking about for -- let's say Mr. Puljic was talking about four, I suppose, jeeps or maybe APC, I don't know, four vehicles of UNPROFOR, and we verified that at the Spanish battalion within the chain of command of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, who had stolen your vehicle in the north, that is, your monitoring mission's vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, you can read that in the report. That was not our vehicle so we were not involved. We only know this whole story from our team M1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. I consulted with my colleagues, and following my cross-examination and if I omit something, they flag those omissions to me. Did you learn eventually who had stolen the vehicles -- sorry, I'm talking about your car, the monitoring mission car.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: You mean from team M1?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Team M1, yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: There is a report about that, so the details I have to read for you then, the details. Let's make clear, there was a daily report and a special report about this event, but that's not in your -- but I know that there is a special report. In my files, there is a special report about the incident in the Jablanica area, what happened to our M1 team, yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We don't have that report here, do we?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I only have your report in which you refer to it and that this vehicle had been stolen by the mujahedins. That's all I have here.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That is what you see. The text here is that what you have, I suppose, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Fine. Tell me, what was your communication with M1 team? Was it daily or did you exchange information before filing reports with your centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, when the M1 team was located, through the week in Jablanica, and came at least once a week, depending on the situation between Jablanica and Mostar, down to the CC in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for my colleague to find this particular report of the M1 team. Witness, I must apologise to you. We have 543.1 exhibit, which is not in the binder we received from the Prosecutor yesterday, but it is in the binders which we had received. That's P543.1, sorry. I'm also going to ask several questions to help us clarify this particular exhibit. You have the document. Witness, let me ask you to please clarify for us the heading. Is this the report from Zenica that is going to the headquarters of the ECMM? Can you help us? It's a special report but I don't know who is sending it to whom.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON WILLEM MARIA VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: This is very interesting because I never saw this. I never saw this. I'm talking about the special report, ECMM report, what our team made, and this is complete something else. This is command of the 1st light assault battalion military police in Mostar. I'm not talking about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Then you were given a wrong document. I apologise. We don't have the same documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [In English] P431.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I think we have the same document now, Witness. Can you clarify for us what kind of special report is this? I see that there's the Mostar province, the Zenica province -- yes, it starts with the Travnik province, and then Mostar province, and then Zenica province. Of course, we're interested in the Mostar province.
